title: A Terraform module hasn't been updated in a long time — how do you upgrade it SAFELY (review current Terraform/provider/module versions and changelogs, check production usage, test in a non-prod environment, and above all scrutinize the `terraform plan`), and why does a `-/+` / "must be replaced" line deserve special attention (a seemingly small change can force resource recreation and downtime)?
shortTitle: Safely upgrading a long-neglected Terraform module, and why a `-/+` "must be replaced" line deserves special scrutiny

s1_definition.profdef: Upgrading a stale Terraform module safely means advancing the module version, the Terraform core version, and the provider versions in controlled, reviewed steps while reading changelogs for breaking changes, validating in a non-production environment first, and treating the `terraform plan` output as the authoritative preview. The `-/+` notation (also printed as "must be replaced") signals that Terraform will DESTROY the existing resource and CREATE a new one because an immutable attribute changed, which for stateful resources means data loss or downtime.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has an old ATM controller that has not been patched in three years. You cannot just rip it out and bolt in the newest model during business hours — Rajesh and Priya are withdrawing cash right now. You read the manufacturer's release notes to learn what changed, you test the new controller in a closed training branch first, and above all you read the installation plan. If the plan says "remove old controller and install new one" (replace) rather than "update firmware in place," that is a red alert, because removing the controller empties the cash cassette and interrupts service. A small-looking spec change can secretly demand a full swap.
s1_definition.oneliner: Upgrade in small reviewed steps and read the plan like a hawk — a `-/+` line means destroy-then-create, which for stateful resources is downtime or data loss.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Upgrading a stale Terraform module safely means advancing the module version, the Terraform core version, and the provider versions in controlled, reviewed steps while reading changelogs for breaking changes, validating in a non-production environment first, and treating the `terraform plan` output as the authoritative preview. The `-/+` notation (also printed as "must be replaced") signals that Terraform will DESTROY the existing resource and CREATE a new one because an immutable attribute changed, which for stateful resources means data loss or downtime.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India has an old ATM controller that has not been patched in three years. You cannot just rip it out and bolt in the newest model during business hours — Rajesh and Priya are withdrawing cash right now. You read the manufacturer's release notes to learn what changed, you test the new controller in a closed training branch first, and above all you read the installation plan. If the plan says "remove old controller and install new one" (replace) rather than "update firmware in place," that is a red alert, because removing the controller empties the cash cassette and interrupts service. A small-looking spec change can secretly demand a full swap.

**One line to remember:** Upgrade in small reviewed steps and read the plan like a hawk — a `-/+` line means destroy-then-create, which for stateful resources is downtime or data loss.

sections.s2_technical:
A Terraform plan prints one of a few symbols for each resource. A `+` means create, a `-` means destroy, a `~` means update in place (safe, no recreation), and `-/+` means destroy then recreate — Terraform even annotates it with `# forces replacement` next to the offending attribute. Update-in-place (`~`) is almost always safe; replacement (`-/+`) is the dangerous one because it physically deletes the resource and makes a new one, which for a database, an EBS volume, or an Elastic IP means the old data or address is gone.

Replacement happens because some attributes are immutable in the cloud API. For example, changing an RDS instance's `engine` or an EC2 instance's `availability_zone`, or a subnet's `cidr_block`, cannot be done in place — AWS has no API to mutate them — so Terraform's only option is destroy-and-recreate. A provider version bump is especially sneaky here: a new provider version may change how an attribute is computed or add a default that differs from the old one, turning a "no-op" into a forced replacement even though you changed nothing in your own HCL.

The safe upgrade workflow has clear steps. First, pin everything before you start, with `required_version` for Terraform core, a `required_providers` version constraint, and a `version` argument on the module source — so you know your current baseline. Second, read the changelog of the module, the provider, and Terraform core between your current version and the target, looking specifically for the words "breaking," "removed," "renamed," and "forces replacement." Third, bump ONE thing at a time (provider first, or module first) rather than everything at once, so when something breaks you know the cause. Fourth, run the upgrade in a non-production workspace or environment with production-like state, and run `terraform plan` there. Fifth — and this is the heart of it — read the plan. If you see any `-/+`, stop and ask whether that recreation is acceptable; for a stateless resource like a security group rule it might be fine, but for an RDS instance it is a data-loss event.

A senior nuance: when you must change an immutable attribute on a resource you cannot afford to lose, you do not just let Terraform replace it. You either use `create_before_destroy` in a `lifecycle` block so the new resource exists before the old one is removed, or you perform a blue-green migration, or you use `terraform state mv` to rename without recreating. And you use `-target` sparingly to apply one resource at a time during a risky upgrade. Another nuance: run `terraform plan -out=plan.bin` and apply that exact saved plan, so what you reviewed is exactly what runs — no drift between review and apply.
sections.s3_banking:
The National Bank of India runs its core ledger on an RDS PostgreSQL instance provisioned by a shared `rds` Terraform module that has not been touched in two years. The platform team wants to upgrade the module to get a newer provider with better encryption defaults. The ledger holds every transaction for Rajesh's SAV2001 and Priya's CUR3001 — it absolutely cannot be destroyed.

Problem 1 — The module bump pulls a new AWS provider whose default for a storage attribute differs from the old one. When the engineer runs plan, a line appears: `instance_class ... # forces replacement`. If applied blindly, the ledger database would be destroyed and recreated empty. This is exactly why `-/+` deserves special attention: a cosmetic-looking version bump silently became a destroy-and-create.

Problem 2 — A security group rule in the same module also shows `-/+`, but recreating a security group rule causes only a sub-second gap and no data loss. So not every replacement is equally dangerous; the engineer must classify each one.

Problem 3 — The engineer must test this in a non-prod environment first and read the saved plan before touching production.

Our runnable Java simulation models a `PlanAnalyzer` that takes a list of `ProposedChange` objects (each with an action and whether it is stateful) and classifies the plan into safe updates, acceptable replacements, and dangerous replacements, refusing to approve if any dangerous replacement is present. Classes: `ProposedChange`, `ChangeAction` enum, `PlanAnalyzer` with `analyze()` and `isSafeToApply()`, and a `ModuleUpgradeDemo` main that feeds a realistic plan and logs the verdict.

##### 4c. Configuration File — the real Terraform pinning this scenario needs

```hcl
# terraform/versions.tf — pin everything so upgrades are deliberate
terraform {
  required_version = "~> 1.6"            # core pinned to 1.6.x

  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "~> 5.31"                 # provider pinned; bump one minor at a time
    }
  }
}
```

```hcl
# terraform/rds.tf — module version pinned; never consumes 'latest'
module "ledger_rds" {
  source  = "git::https://git.nbi.internal/modules/rds.git?ref=v3.2.0"  # exact tag

  identifier     = "nbi-core-ledger"
  engine         = "postgres"
  instance_class = "db.r6g.2xlarge"

  # Protect a stateful resource from accidental destroy-and-recreate
  lifecycle {
    prevent_destroy       = true          # plan errors if a -/+ would destroy it
    create_before_destroy = true          # if replacement is truly needed, build new first
  }
}
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build and run the plan-analysis simulation
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -cp target/classes com.bank.iac.ModuleUpgradeDemo

# The real safe-upgrade workflow:
cd terraform
terraform init -upgrade                 # pull the new module/provider versions
terraform plan -out=upgrade.plan        # save the exact plan you will review
terraform show upgrade.plan | grep -A2 "forces replacement"   # hunt for -/+ lines
# Review in a NON-PROD workspace first:
terraform workspace select nonprod
terraform apply upgrade.plan            # apply the exact reviewed plan
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: a module upgrade from v3.2.0 to v4.0.0 that also bumps the AWS provider, producing a plan with three changes — an RDS instance replacement, a security-group-rule replacement, and a parameter-group in-place update.

Step 1: The engineer runs the upgrade in a non-prod workspace and saves the plan to a file, so the reviewed plan and the applied plan are guaranteed identical.

Step 2: The analyzer reads the first change, the RDS instance, and sees the action is REPLACE and the resource is stateful. This is the dangerous case — recreating it would delete the ledger. The analyzer marks the whole plan unsafe.

Step 3: The analyzer reads the second change, a security-group-rule replacement. The action is also REPLACE but the resource is stateless, so recreating it causes only a momentary gap and no data loss. It is logged as acceptable, not fatal.

Step 4: The analyzer reads the third change, a parameter-group update in place. This is a `~` action, fully safe, logged as safe.

Step 5: Because one stateful replacement was found, the final verdict is NOT safe. The apply is aborted, the ledger is protected, and the engineer is told to use create-before-destroy or a blue-green migration before re-planning.

```
2026-10-30 01:35:02 [INFO   ] National Bank of India — upgrading stale 'rds' module v3.2.0 -> v4.0.0
2026-10-30 01:35:02 [INFO   ] Reading plan from NON-PROD workspace before touching prod ledger...
2026-10-30 01:35:02 [SEVERE ]   -/+ module.ledger_rds.aws_db_instance.this — REPLACE of STATEFUL resource! instance_class attribute recomputed by new provider forces replacement => DATA LOSS / DOWNTIME. BLOCK.
2026-10-30 01:35:02 [WARNING]   -/+ module.ledger_rds.aws_security_group_rule.ingress — replace of stateless resource (description change forces rule replacement) — brief gap, usually acceptable
2026-10-30 01:35:02 [INFO   ]   ~ module.ledger_rds.aws_db_parameter_group.this — update in place (safe)
2026-10-30 01:35:02 [SEVERE ] Verdict: plan is NOT safe — a stateful resource would be replaced. Use create_before_destroy / state mv / blue-green instead.
2026-10-30 01:35:02 [SEVERE ] Aborting apply. Ledger database SAV2001/CUR3001 transactions protected.
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Upgrading a Terraform module that has sat untouched for a long time is a controlled change process, not a one-shot command. I start by pinning my current baseline — the Terraform core version with required_version, the provider with a required_providers constraint, and the module with an exact version tag on its source — so I know precisely where I am before I move. Then I read the changelogs for the module, the provider, and Terraform core between my current and target versions, searching specifically for the words breaking, removed, renamed, and forces replacement. I bump one thing at a time, I test in a non-production environment that has production-like state, and above everything else I read the terraform plan.

The reason the plan matters so much is the difference between the symbols it prints. A tilde means update in place and is almost always safe. A minus-plus, which Terraform also prints as "must be replaced," means Terraform will destroy the existing resource and create a brand new one, because some immutable attribute changed that the cloud API cannot mutate in place. That is the line I scrutinise, because a seemingly trivial change — even a provider version bump that recomputes a default — can silently force the recreation of a resource.

Why that is dangerous depends entirely on whether the resource is stateful. In my project at the National Bank of India, we upgraded a two-year-old rds module and the plan showed a minus-plus on the core ledger database, driven by nothing more than the new provider recomputing the instance class. If I had applied that blindly, the database holding every transaction for Rajesh's SAV2001 and Priya's CUR3001 would have been destroyed and recreated empty. The same plan also had a minus-plus on a security group rule, but that is stateless, so recreating it was just a sub-second gap. I classify every replacement by blast radius, I protect stateful resources with prevent_destroy and create_before_destroy, and when a stateful resource genuinely must change an immutable attribute I do a blue-green migration or a state move rather than letting Terraform destroy it. The principle I always state is that a clean-looking version bump is never automatically safe — the plan, read line by line, is the only truth.
